video.title: Why Your Serve is So Slow

classification.reason: The coach provides executable drills and cues, such as nestling the racket into the V of the hand, throwing the racket out to the hitting side, and using the clock drill progression.

problem.title_as_question: Why is your overhead and serve so slow and weak?
problem.definition: Players struggle to generate speed on overheads and serves because their mental model focuses on throwing the racket up at the ball or hitting over the net, rather than throwing the racket out to the side with proper palm connection.
problem.target_player: Players who get stuck in the back scratch, flex their wrist over the top, or lack explosive racket speed on overheads and serves

symptoms.description: Very low ball velocity on overheads or serves, around 80 mph or lower, with frequent mishits or whiffs.
Racket speed stalls as the player gets slow and stuck in the back scratch position.
Player flexes the wrist over the top of the ball instead of naturally pronating and externally/internally rotating.

causes.statement: The player attempts to throw the racket up or down-and-up directly at the ball rather than throwing it out to the hitting side.
The brain is psychologically anchored on clearing the net, preventing a committed and free outward release.
The racket is not nestled deep into the V of the hand and index palm, preventing relaxed control and inertia perception of the racket face.
The player fails to recognize that the overhead/serve uses the exact same outward release and flip mechanics as the forehand along a different plane.

angles.summary: Thinking the racket must be swung upward toward the ball is incorrect; the racket naturally stretches forward and up by being thrown out to the hitting side.
The body orientation and outward throwing motion near the net mimic the biomechanics of a baseball pitcher.
Top players like Taylor Fritz on serves, and Sinner, Federer, and Alcaraz on forehands, reset their grip deep into the V of the palm before swinging.
The clock drill conceptualizes swings at different heights as points along the hands of a clock sharing the same core release motion.

solutions.summary: Cue yourself to throw the racket out to your hitting side (right for righties, left for lefties) rather than up at the ball.
solutions.external_goal: Throw racket out to the hitting side

solutions.summary: Stand right next to the net and hit fed overheads from a low contact zone, throwing the racket outward like a baseball pitcher without worrying about clearing the net.
solutions.external_goal: Throw the racket through the contact zone right at the net

solutions.summary: Nestle the racket handle deep into the V of the hand and index palm, pulling the bottom fingers off the handle during preparation to calibrate feel.
solutions.external_goal: Nestle racket into hand V with bottom fingers peeling off

solutions.summary: Practice the clock drill: start with low forehands throwing the racket out, progress higher along the clock face, and switch to a continental grip as contact goes overhead while keeping the same flip feel.
solutions.external_goal: Swing outward at every hour mark along the clock continuum
